On CoNLL with LLaMA, LP leads AUROC (0.761) yet trails in $\rho$ (0.307), confirming this pattern across datasets.

\paragraph{Signal rankings shift with task difficulty.}
On CoNLL (greedy F1${\approx}$0.91), EM leads ($\rho{=}0.451$, AUROC${=}0.816$), surpassing SJ and VC.
When most samples are near-correct, binary agreement captures remaining variance more efficiently than set-level similarity.
This crossover---EM${>}$SJ on easy tasks vs.\ SJ${>}$EM on hard tasks---demonstrates difficulty-dependent complementarity rather than a universal structural advantage, suggesting practitioners should match signal type to expected task difficulty.
Stability across the two model families (both 8B) is strong: SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.436$ (Qwen) vs.\ $0.431$ (LLaMA) on CoNLL ($\Delta{=}0.005$, within 3-seed $\sigma{\approx}0.007$).
On WNUT-17 ($N{=}16$), where 52\% of instances receive zero F1, full-set correlations are misleading: VC achieves $\rho{=}0.724$ (AUROC${=}0.913$), but this is entirely driven by the zero/non-zero boundary (conditional $\rho{=}0.038$, n.s.; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}).
LP exhibits strong \textit{negative} correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$, AUROC${=}0.219$).
We hypothesize that this reversal reflects overconfidence on out-of-distribution inputs \citep{xiong2024llm}: the model assigns high log-probabilities to fluent but incorrect entity patterns (e.g., common noun phrases that resemble but do not match rare WNUT entity types), while producing lower scores for genuinely uncertain outputs where it correctly hedges.
On the conditional set, all signals collapse toward weak or non-significant correlations ($\rho{\leq}0.35$), with SJ achieving only $\rho{=}0.089$ ($p{=}0.020$) on the full set---suggesting a capability boundary beyond which consistency signals capture binary success/failure but not quality gradation.

\paragraph{Conditional filtering.}
Filtering to non-zero F1 instances separates binary success detection (can the model extract \textit{anything}?) from quality gradation (among successful extractions, which are better?), but excludes the hardest instances where models fail completely---the conditional set is easier on average.
This reshuffles signal rankings (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}, right).
EM emerges as the strongest conditional signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.360$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.417$; preliminary), while VC and FK drop substantially (VC NER: $0.379{\to}0.300$; FK NER: $0.267{\to}0.176$).
LP RE collapses to $\rho{=}0.011$, confirming its full-set correlation was driven by zero/non-zero separation.
This creates a natural complementarity: VC and SJ are preferred on the full set, while EM provides the most precise ranking within the non-trivial subset (see Appendix~\ref{app:additional} for details).

We anchor this analysis on SciERC, where output diversity is substantial: only 11--18\% of instances produce identical outputs across all $N{=}8$ samples, with 39--43\% unique outputs per instance (mean 3.5 distinct outputs), per-sample F1 standard deviation of 0.11--0.14, and mean pairwise SJ of 0.703.

\paragraph{No significant improvement over greedy.}
We evaluate significance via 3-seed instance-level paired bootstrap resampling ($B{=}10{,}000$, Fisher combination; $n{=}551$).
On NER, the oracle (0.745, 3-seed mean) reveals 12.5~pp of headroom above greedy (0.620).
LP achieves the highest mean selection F1 (0.620), indistinguishable from greedy ($\Delta{=}{+}0.0$~pp, Fisher $p{=}0.54$).
On RE, the best signal (LP, 0.395) falls below greedy (0.404, $-0.9$\,pp, $p{=}0.80$; single seed), while 18.1~pp of oracle headroom remains; cross-seed analysis confirms RE LP failures are partially systematic (Appendix~\ref{app:lp_failure_stability}).
TOST equivalence testing confirms most signals are indistinguishable from greedy at ${\pm}2$--$3$~pp on NER; on RE, EM and VC fail equivalence even at ${\pm}5$~pp (Table~\ref{tab:tost}, Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}).
VC ($\rho{=}0.379$, the best quality estimator) selects---via majority-threshold voting, distinct from the continuous QE score---to only 0.595 on NER (3-seed mean), \textit{significantly below} greedy ($\Delta{=}{-}2.5$~pp, Fisher $p{<}0.001$).
The gap extends to CoNLL at $N{=}8$ (ceiling effect, 57--88\% identical outputs) and WNUT-17 (capability boundary; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).

\paragraph{Seed variability.}
While the 3-seed mean confirms the gap direction, individual seeds exhibit notable variance.
Seed~456 produces uniformly negative selection deltas across all five signals (VC $-3.4$~pp, EM $-2.0$~pp, SJ $-1.6$~pp, FK $-1.5$~pp, LP $-0.3$~pp), whereas seeds~42 and~123 show mixed behavior with LP achieving modest positive deltas ($+0.6$ and $-0.2$~pp respectively).
This variability does not undermine the central finding: even the most favorable single seed (seed~42, LP $\Delta{=}{+}0.6$~pp) falls short of significance ($p{=}0.19$), and the gap direction is consistent across all seeds for instance-level signals.
The seed sensitivity underscores that single-seed selection evaluations---common in the literature---may overstate or understate signal utility by several percentage points, motivating our multi-seed design.

\paragraph{Quality estimation $\neq$ output selection.}
Instance-level confidence signals predict \textit{which inputs} the model handles reliably, not \textit{which output} among $N$ candidates is best.
When per-sample variance is low relative to instance-level difficulty, even perfect quality estimation cannot discriminate among near-identical candidates.
This gap has direct consequences for test-time scaling in IE \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}: closing it likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}.

%% ============================================================

\label{sec:robustness_main}

Consistency-based signals show robust performance across $T{\in}\{0.7, 1.0\}$ (SJ NER $\Delta\rho{=}0.028$, bootstrap CI includes zero) and sublinear gains from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, with structural signals maintaining their advantage over LP across all NER settings ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.135$ to ${+}0.175$; Table~\ref{tab:robustness}, Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).
On RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.012$, preliminary).
NER signals are reasonably calibrated (ECE 0.069--0.096; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}), while RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339) and compound errors impose a ceiling at $\rho{\approx}0.28$ for $N{=}16$.

Our evaluation covers three datasets but only one RE benchmark (SciERC), where 40\% of instances receive zero F1, compressing the discriminable range and limiting signal differentiation for relation extraction.
RE selection failure persists even when restricting to non-zero F1 instances (Appendix~\ref{app:re_conditional_selection}), ruling out floor effects as the sole explanation, but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated.
WNUT-17 confirms the capability boundary of our approach, but our positive results on formal-domain text (CoNLL, SciERC) have not been validated on informal or noisy text where models achieve non-trivial performance.

We evaluate two model families (Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B), both at 8B parameters.
A 3-seed robustness analysis confirms that signal rankings are stable across seeds ($\sigma{\leq}0.026$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}), but whether our findings---particularly the correlation-selection gap and the difficulty-dependent signal ordering---hold for larger models (70B+) or closed-source APIs remains untested.
Larger models may produce higher-quality and more diverse samples, potentially altering the signal landscape.

Our analysis of selection potential uses only unsupervised signals.
We do not train a dedicated verifier or reward model, leaving unknown how much of the oracle headroom a supervised approach could recover.

We evaluate at $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$.
The behavior of confidence signals at larger sample sizes (e.g., $N{=}64$ or $N{=}128$) is unknown, and $N$-scaling gains are setting-dependent: SJ improves by $+0.047$ on Qwen SciERC NER but only $+0.016$ on LLaMA SciERC NER when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$.

On CoNLL with LLaMA, the SJ--FK gap is only 0.003 ($\rho{=}0.431$ vs.\ $0.428$), so the structural advantage over surface signals may not generalize to all simple-schema datasets.
Our free-form ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that LP score compression persists without constrained decoding, but was conducted on a single dataset (SciERC) with one model (Qwen3-8B); whether the compression finding generalizes to other datasets, model families, or model scales remains untested.

Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with \texttt{enable\_thinking} active, injecting empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks (4--5 tokens, no reasoning chain) before each response; CoNLL and WNUT checkpoints disabled this feature.
At inference time, constrained decoding suppresses thinking tokens in all configurations, so they do not appear in generated samples.
The empty blocks may weakly affect first-token probability distributions during training, potentially shifting LP score calibration on SciERC; however, since LP selection fails across all datasets including CoNLL and WNUT-17 (which lack this confound), the thinking token inconsistency is unlikely to explain the correlation-selection gap.
The absence of any reasoning content further limits the representational impact.

Finally, log-probability was excluded from the temperature comparison ($T{=}0.7$ vs.\ $T{=}1.0$) due to missing $T{=}0.7$ LP data; all LP compression analyses use $T{=}1.0$ exclusively, and whether compression behavior changes at lower temperatures remains unknown.
The free-form ablation (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$) provides stronger evidence that compression is not an artifact of the decoding strategy, but does not address temperature as a variable.
Since practitioners commonly deploy at $T{<}1.0$ for reliability, this untested dependence represents a gap between our evaluation conditions ($T{=}1.0$) and typical deployment settings.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and aggregating them---has become a powerful strategy for improving language model reasoning.
On discrete-answer tasks such as arithmetic and commonsense QA, majority voting over chain-of-thought samples yields large gains: +18 percentage points on GSM8K (PaLM-540B; \citealp{wang2023selfconsistency}).
More broadly, test-time compute scaling through repeated sampling and selection has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling, offering substantial quality improvements at inference time \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
These results rest on a shared assumption: that among $N$ stochastic samples, a selection mechanism can identify better outputs.
For tasks with a single correct answer, this assumption holds naturally---the majority vote is the selector.
But information extraction (IE) poses a fundamentally different challenge.
The output is not a single token or number; it is a \textit{set} of entities or relations with internal dependencies, where two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical structures.
There is no obvious majority to vote on, partial agreement is the norm rather than the exception, and the space of valid outputs is combinatorially large.
Can self-consistency still provide useful signal in this structured setting?

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated two distinct objectives: \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) and \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
These require different signal properties: the former benefits from instance-level aggregation, while the latter demands per-sample discrimination.
Self-consistency methods for discrete answers \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc} and weighted variants \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence---an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
The most relevant study, \citet{nedellec2026consistency}, examines consistency--accuracy correlations for LLM-based IE, finding results that our quality-estimation analysis corroborates.
Our work extends theirs in three directions: (i)~structural matching beyond surface-level agreement, (ii)~testing whether quality estimation translates to best-of-$N$ selection (it does not), and (iii)~a difficulty gradient revealing non-obvious findings---WNUT-17 conditional correlations collapse to $\rho{=}0.038$ (n.s.) and LP exhibits strong \textit{negative} correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$)---that would be invisible on a single dataset.

Structured IE requires schema-compliant output, making constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided} the standard inference strategy---without it, a substantial fraction of outputs from general-purpose models are unparseable.\footnote{Fine-tuned models may retain format compliance without grammar constraints: our free-form ablation achieves 99.95\% valid JSON rate (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).}
All experiments use constrained decoding, the regime under which structured IE is practically deployed.

Our central finding is the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (Figure~\ref{fig:overview}): consistency-based signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75) but fail at sample selection despite 12--18~pp of oracle headroom.
Four of five signals are instance-level by construction---this is definitional, not empirical.
The non-trivial questions are whether (a)~consensus-proximity selection, instantiating MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, freitag2022high, muller2021understanding}, can recover per-sample discrimination, and (b)~whether log-probability, the only per-sample signal, can exploit the headroom.
Both fail: MBR utility correlates with F1 across instances but not within them (\S\ref{sec:discussion}); log-probability scores are severely compressed (60\% of instances effectively tied), though where compression is mitigated, LP becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$).
A controlled free-form decoding ablation confirms that NER LP compression persists without constrained decoding; on RE, LP selection reverses direction (preliminary), revealing task-dependent interaction with decoding regime (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: high inter-sample agreement correlates with high F1 (quality estimation). \textbf{Right}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all candidates, precluding sample selection.}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We systematically compare five confidence signals from three families---structural (entity voting confidence [VC], Soft Jaccard [SJ]), surface (exact match [EM], Fleiss' $\kappa$ [FK]), and model-internal (log-probability [LP])---across NER and RE on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}, using Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B.
Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Evaluation methodology.}
    We compare five confidence signals from three families---structural, surface, and model-internal---across three distinct metrics: quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1).
    These metrics decouple: EM leads AUROC (0.749) but ranks third in $\rho$ (0.295), so single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal for a given use case.

    \item \textbf{The correlation-selection gap: diagnosis.}
    All signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75) yet none significantly improves selection despite 12--18~pp of oracle headroom.
    The failure of four instance-level signals is definitional---they assign a single score per input and cannot rank candidates by construction.
    The empirical contribution is diagnosing why the two per-sample mechanisms that \textit{could} bridge the gap both fail: log-probability scores are compressed into effective ties (60\% of instances within $\varepsilon{=}0.05$), and consensus-proximity selection (MBR decoding) correlates with quality across instances but not within them.
    Where compression is mitigated, LP becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$), confirming score compression as the primary bottleneck.
    A controlled ablation confirms LP compression persists without constrained decoding on NER; on RE, LP selection reverses direction (preliminary), indicating task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.

    \item \textbf{Task-complexity boundary conditions.}
    Signal rankings shift with task difficulty: EM leads on easy tasks, SJ on hard tasks---consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
    At the capability boundary (WNUT-17, 52\% zero F1), conditional correlations collapse to non-significance and LP exhibits strong negative correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$)---phenomena invisible on a single dataset that extend \citet{nedellec2026consistency}'s quality-estimation analysis.
    NER findings span three datasets; RE conclusions rest on SciERC alone (preliminary).
\end{enumerate}

The free-form ablation (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$) provides stronger evidence that compression is not an artifact of the decoding strategy, but does not address temperature as a variable.
Since practitioners commonly deploy at $T{<}1.0$ for reliability, this untested dependence represents a gap between our evaluation conditions ($T{=}1.0$) and typical deployment settings.
Lower temperatures concentrate probability mass on fewer tokens, which could either reduce LP compression (by widening score gaps between high- and low-probability sequences) or exacerbate it (by collapsing diversity so that all $N$ samples share near-identical token-level likelihoods).
The direction of this interaction is not predictable from first principles and depends on how the model's likelihood surface interacts with the structured output space.
Resolving this would require a controlled $T$-sweep with LP data at each temperature, which our experimental pipeline did not collect.

\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency---sampling multiple outputs and selecting via agreement---yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but information extraction (IE) produces \textit{sets} of entities and relations with partial overlap, where no majority vote exists.
Can consistency signals nonetheless select the best among $N$ candidates?

Across three NER and one RE benchmark with two 8B-parameter models, all signals achieve strong quality estimation yet none significantly improves sample selection despite 12--18~pp of oracle headroom---the \textit{correlation-selection gap}.
Instance-level signals fail by construction; the two mechanisms that \textit{could} bridge the gap also fail: log-probability scores are compressed into effective ties (60\% of instances), and consensus-proximity selection (MBR decoding) correlates with quality across but not within instances.
Signal rankings are difficulty-dependent and collapse at the capability boundary.

The gap widens with sample size; closing it likely requires per-sample scoring such as trained verifiers.
\end{abstract}

36	Our contributions are:
37	\begin{enumerate}
38	    \item \textbf{Multi-metric evaluation revealing metric dissociation.}
39	    We compare five confidence signals from three families---structural, surface, and model-internal---across three distinct metrics: quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1).
40	    These metrics decouple: EM leads AUROC (0.749) but ranks third in $\rho$ (0.295), so single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal for a given use case.
41	
42	    \item \textbf{LP score compression and MBR utility-quality misalignment.}
43	    All signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75) yet none significantly improves selection despite 12--18~pp of oracle headroom.
44	    The failure of four instance-level signals is definitional---they assign a single score per input and cannot rank candidates by construction.
45	    The empirical contribution is diagnosing why the two per-sample mechanisms that \textit{could} bridge the gap both fail: log-probability scores are compressed into effective ties (60\% of instances within $\varepsilon{=}0.05$), and consensus-proximity selection (MBR decoding) correlates with quality across instances but not within them.
46	    Where compression is mitigated, LP becomes a significant selector ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$), confirming score compression as the primary bottleneck.
47	    A controlled ablation confirms LP compression persists without constrained decoding on NER; on RE, LP selection reverses direction (preliminary), indicating task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.
48	
49	    \item \textbf{Task-complexity boundary conditions.}
50	    Signal rankings shift with task difficulty: EM leads on easy tasks, SJ on hard tasks---consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.
51	    At the capability boundary (WNUT-17, 52\% zero F1), conditional correlations collapse to non-significance and LP exhibits strong negative correlation ($\rho{=}{-}0.410$)---phenomena invisible on a single dataset that extend \citet{nedellec2026consistency}'s quality-estimation analysis.
52	    NER findings span three datasets; RE conclusions rest on SciERC alone (preliminary).
53	\end{enumerate}

# Rho Consistency Audit Report

**Date**: 2026-05-15
**Trigger**: Reviewer flagged large discrepancies between registry rho values and bootstrap CI rho values

## Root Cause

The discrepancy comes from two different evaluation pipelines using different instance filtering:

### Old Pipeline (`compute_metrics.py`)
- **No filtering**: uses ALL instances including gold-empty ones
- **FK bug**: `compute_fk()` returns 0.0 when all samples predict no entities (should be 1.0 = perfect agreement on empty set)
- **F1 convention**: returns 0.0 when tp=0, including when both pred and gold are empty

### New Pipeline (`eval_n16_5signal.py`, `fk_bootstrap_ci.py`, `analyze_exp017_*.py`)
- **Filters out gold-empty instances**: `len(gold.get("entities", [])) > 0`
- **Uses `consistency.py`**: `fleiss_kappa_surface()` returns 1.0 for all-empty (correct)
- **Reports n_valid** separate from n_total

### Mechanism of Inflation / Deflation

For CoNLL2003 (3453 test sentences), **697 instances (20.2%) have zero gold entities**.

For these gold-empty instances in the old pipeline:
- All samples typically predict few/no entities → **FK ≈ 0.04** (buggy), **F1 = 0.0**
- All samples agree on empty output → **SJ ≈ 0.98**, **F1 = 0.0**

Adding 697 points at (FK≈0, F1=0) creates a strong artificial cluster that inflates Spearman rho for FK.
Adding 697 points at (SJ≈1, F1=0) creates an anti-correlated cluster that deflates Spearman rho for SJ.

This is why FK rho jumped from 0.48 to 0.81, while SJ rho dropped from 0.48 to 0.18 — a complete **rank reversal**.

## Affected Experiments

| exp_id | Signal | Old (registry) | New (correct) | Delta | Instance Change |
|--------|--------|----------------|---------------|-------|-----------------|
| exp_017_llama_conll_n16_r1024 | FK | **0.8095** | **0.4752** | -0.3343 | 3453→2756 |

file.content:
Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with \texttt{enable\_thinking} active, injecting empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks (4--5 tokens, no reasoning chain) before each response; CoNLL and WNUT checkpoints disabled this feature.
At inference time, constrained decoding suppresses thinking tokens in all configurations, so they do not appear in generated samples.
The empty blocks may weakly affect first-token probability distributions during training, potentially shifting LP score calibration on SciERC; however, since LP selection fails across all datasets including CoNLL and WNUT-17 (which lack this confound), the thinking token inconsistency is unlikely to explain the correlation-selection gap.
The absence of any reasoning content further limits the representational impact.

Finally, log-probability was excluded from the temperature comparison ($T{=}0.7$ vs.\ $T{=}1.0$) due to missing $T{=}0.7$ LP data; all LP compression analyses use $T{=}1.0$ exclusively, and whether compression behavior changes at lower temperatures remains unknown.
The free-form ablation (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$) provides stronger evidence that compression is not an artifact of the decoding strategy, but does not address temperature as a variable.
Since practitioners commonly deploy at $T{<}1.0$ for reliability, this untested dependence represents a gap between our evaluation conditions ($T{=}1.0$) and typical deployment settings.
Lower temperatures concentrate probability mass on fewer tokens, which could either reduce LP compression (by widening score gaps between high- and low-probability sequences) or exacerbate it (by collapsing diversity so that all $N$ samples share near-identical token-level likelihoods).
The direction of this interaction is not predictable from first principles and depends on how the model's likelihood surface interacts with the structured output space.
Resolving this would require a controlled $T$-sweep with LP data at each temperature, which our experimental pipeline did not collect.
